piece.caption:
How to screen vendor contracts for late payment penalties using AI tools before signing.

When signing supplier or contractor agreements, hidden penalty clauses can cost you heavily. Large legal organizations like Ropes & Gray and Legora use AI for a first pass review, categorizing documents and surfacing key risks across contract sets. You can adopt this exact method: run a targeted prompt on any contract text to flag non-standard payment terms or automatic renewal traps. Remember, AI only does the initial diligence, human verification remains essential before signing.

Comment CONTRACT for the exact screening prompt.

piece.dm_text:
Here is the contract screening framework used for legal diligence:

1. Copy your contract text into ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini.
2. Paste this screening prompt: 'Act as a contract reviewer. Analyze this agreement and list all clauses related to: (a) late payment interest rates or daily penalties, (b) automatic contract renewal terms, (c) unilateral termination rights. Highlight any terms that seem strict or non-standard.'
3. Review the flagged lines against your actual document before signing.

Note: As noted by firms like Ropes & Gray, AI only provides a first pass summary; human verification is mandatory for final decisions.

[45] OpenAI News — How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence
URL: https://openai.com/index/ropes-gray-ai-diligence
How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence | OpenAI OpenAI October 29, 2026
Law firm Ropes & Gray is developing a transactional diligence AI tool in partnership with OpenAI.
Share In transactional diligence, lawyers need to work through large volumes of documents under tight deadlines. Ropes & Gray was an early adopter of AI in the legal industry, and in partnership with OpenAI, they are now developing a proprietary AI tool to provide more expertise to more clients.
Building a first pass for commercial contract diligence
Before finalizing any acquisition, the buyer must carry out a thorough investigation to validate the seller’s financial and legal claims. That process of transactional diligence uncovers risks and liabilities, requiring data-heavy research that usually involves an entire team of lawyers.
From parsing through an enormous number of documents to analyzing patterns, putting together a bid on a short timeline can take days of intensive work. To help their lawyers help their clients move more quickly, Ropes & Gray developed a transactional diligence AI tool with OpenAI.
“It’s enabling all the lawyers at our firm to actually get to what we’re supposed to be doing,” says Howard Glazer, the Partner and Head of Practice AI at Ropes & Gray. “Our clients don’t pay us to review contracts. They pay us to make judgments based on what’s in the contracts.”
The new diligence AI tool takes a first pass by combing through thousands of pages, identifying relevant documents and automatically grouping them together based on themes and issues. Along with the research, the tool produces summaries and a completed report in Ropes & Gray’s signature format. It inventories and categorizes a data room, so it can review full relationships, not isolated documents. Of course, lawyers can inspect the grouping and categorization to confirm nothing is missed.
The initial development work has focused on material commercial contracts. In working sessions, Ropes & Gray’s lawyers compared test outputs with human-authored diligence reports from completed deals, then refined the rubric and report format based on what the drafts got right and where they fell short.
Ropes & Gray designed the tool with a consistent query and framework that mimics the exact steps their team would take, from initial reviews to summaries to higher-level reviews. Comparable to the work of a capable junior-to-mid-level associate, this tool gives their firm consistently high-quality work that serves as a first pass through the process.
“Our lawyers still need to review everything,” says Lichtenstein. “Because anything that we’re going to deliver to a client, we need to be able to stand behind 100%. This is why the tool is designed to allow lawyers to easily review interim summaries and actual documents.” With the initial review taken care of, lawyers can spend more time reviewing and refining the work, resulting in a more carefully crafted final judgment.
Ropes & Gray has publicly described an ambition for the tool to produce a detailed, issue-level diligence report in hours rather than weeks.
With tools like their proprietary diligence tool and GPT‑6 Astra, Ropes & Gray has been able to solve client problems far faster than before.
The tool inventories and categorizes a data room, grouping related documents by themes and issues.
The workflow produces summaries and a report in Ropes & Gray’s format.
Lawyers review interim summaries and source documents before delivering work to clients.
Testing compares draft outputs with lawyer-authored diligence reports to refine the rubric and report format.
Lichtenstein and Glazer offer two lessons from their experience with AI.
Experiment with using AI for everything. From finding dress shoes to vibecoding games for his kids, Lichtenstein has been using AI in every facet of his life. “Just by using it for so many different things, I feel like I’ve learned a lot of what it does well, how you can make it work better,” Lichtenstein explains. “The most rewarding part is not when it does well, it’s when you see the mistake and try to figure out what to do. That’s where it transformed from something I was playing with to a really powerful professional tool.”
Put the clients first. While designing AI tools and workflows, Ropes & Gray emphasizes the importance of keeping the firm’s greatest goal in mind. “It’s exciting to think there is so much opportunity, but only if we learn how to use it and make sure that our clients are the ones who are winning,” says Glazer. “That’s what we’re focused on: how can we use this to benefit the clients? And if we do that, then everything will work out fine.”
While today, AI is helping Ropes & Gray with legal diligence, Glazer believes that the next stage of AI will help create collective knowledge within the firm.
With 340 partners and 1500 lawyers, Ropes & Gray sees value in creating access to every person’s knowledge, from their client meetings to past projects, to better solve client problems.
“That’s not just saving time. It’s not just saving money,” says Glazer. “It’s using the AI tools to directly create value, and that’s just amazing.”

[49] OpenAI News — Legora is building the agentic operating system for legal work
URL: https://openai.com/index/legora
Legora is building the agentic operating system for legal work | OpenAI OpenAI October 28, 2026
Powered by OpenAI models and coding agents, Legora helps legal teams move faster, broaden analysis and focus on higher-value work.
reduction in Legora legal-team time spent reviewing NDAs
faster contract turnaround for a Fortune 100 customer
Share Building for a profession where time—and trust—are scarce
Founded in Stockholm in 2023, Legora ⁠ (opens in a new window) is building what CEO and co-founder Max Junestrand calls “the agentic operating system for legal work”: bringing AI into the workflows lawyers rely on every day.
The company started with the insight that legal teams are unusually time crunched, meaning some valuable work doesn’t get done. Think of the junior lawyer told to review an impossible number of contracts overnight and only able to focus on a fraction.
Legora can provide those services “on tap”, which is why Junestrand’s ambition is that every piece of legal work in the world should run on his platform. OpenAI has been part of that journey from the beginning: the release of GPT‑3.5 was the moment many of the legal use cases the founding team had been experimenting with became possible. Today, OpenAI is a key model provider for Legora, powering core workflows across its legal AI platform, from agentic legal work to large-scale document review. Legora builds on new OpenAI model capabilities as they become available, translating advances in intelligence into what lawyers can accomplish with its product.
An AI-native company building an AI-native product
Legora’s use of AI goes beyond the product it sells, and has expanded its use of ChatGPT Work, Codex and dots across its own teams. OpenAI’s technology is becoming part of both the product Legora builds for its customers as well as shaping how the company itself operates. “It’s incredibly important to me that we stay as AI-native as possible,” confirms Junestrand.
For Jacob Lauritzen, CTO at Legora, coding agents have changed how quickly the engineering team can develop new ideas. Instead of researching one possible solution and committing engineering time before knowing whether it’s the right path, teams can prototype many approaches at once. “We can explore 20 solutions at the same time and, within days, pick the one we know will be the best.”
The same approach changes how Legora responds when something goes wrong. Previously, diagnosing a product issue could mean several engineers investigating different possible causes over a number of hours. Coding agents can now search millions of lines of logs and pursue many possible explanations simultaneously, sometimes taking Legora from bug report to working fix in around five minutes .
Customers, of course, don’t see the engineering efficiency itself. But they do experience the results: problems can be resolved faster, feedback can reach product teams sooner, and new ideas can be tested with customers earlier in the development cycle.
Giving Legora’s own lawyers room to do higher-value work
Legora’s own legal team experiences the same transformation its product is designed to create for customers. General Counsel Emma Kadri Bergström points to the example of NDAs. Her team analysed the agreements they had historically signed and built a playbook that allows Legora to take a first pass at incoming NDAs, highlighting terms that fall outside acceptable parameters.
Before the workflow was introduced, Kadri Bergström estimates that reviewing these “boring documents” consumed around 20% of the legal team’s capacity . Today, it’s under 1% .
That reclaimed time matters because the company itself is scaling rapidly. In the past year, Kadri Bergström says the business has expanded from three offices to 18 , completed three financing rounds and made five acquisitions . The legal team has had to support that growth while remaining closely connected to the business.
AI has also allowed the team to take on work that might previously have been outsourced or narrowed because of limited capacity. In M&A diligence, for example, agents can begin reviewing contracts and surfacing information across the deal set, with lawyers reviewing and interpreting the output.
“AI doesn’t just make you faster. It also increases quality.”
From faster review to broader, higher-quality analysis
For Legora’s customers, the opportunity isn’t simply to complete the same work faster. AI has also increased the scope of work that can be taken on.
Alex Fortescue-Webb, Global Head of Legal Engineering, points to due diligence as an example. In a traditional review, time and cost constraints can force teams to concentrate deeply on only the most valuable contracts. Legora’s Tabular Review workflow can analyse thousands of contracts across multiple questions in minutes, allowing lawyers to apply detailed scrutiny much more broadly.
That can alter the quality of the final work. Risks that might previously have sat in contracts outside the manually reviewed subset can now be surfaced for a lawyer to assess.
The results are already measurable. Junestrand cites one Fortune 100 customer that has:
saved more than $20 million on external litigation and diligence
returned 9.5 hours per lawyer each week for higher-value work
Through the Legora plugin for ChatGPT ⁠ , legal teams can also use Legora’s capabilities within their ChatGPT conversations .

Start with the problem. Focus on what people need to accomplish, then determine where AI can improve the workflow.
Build a network of champions. Internal advocates help turn experimentation into sustained adoption.
Be ready to rebuild. As models improve, yesterday’s product assumptions can quickly become outdated.
Design for trust. Build evaluation, testing and transparency into the experience from the start.
For Legora, the next frontier isn’t just making today’s legal workflows faster. It’s expanding the kinds of work AI can take on, while making collaboration between lawyers and AI increasingly natural.
Jacob Lauritzen sees two advances happening in parallel. First, agents will be able to tackle longer-running tasks that require far greater context and autonomy. He imagines due diligence spanning millions of pages running overnight, with the analysis ready for a lawyer to review when they arrive the next morning.
At the same time, increasingly capable models are becoming faster. That opens up a different kind of experience: real-time collaboration where a lawyer and AI can work back and forth on a contract, analysis or piece of advice rather than treating
